title: Prompt Engineering
description: Structured prompting techniques for reliably controlling LLM behavior.
blurb: Structured prompting techniques for reliably controlling LLM behavior.
careerApplications: Prompt engineering is the fastest, cheapest lever for improving an LLM application's reliability, and is expected working knowledge for any AI-adjacent engineering role today.

lessons.title: What prompting is & instruction clarity
objectives: Write a clear, unambiguous instruction for an LLM
Explain how prompting as control surface changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect prompting as control surface with instruction specificity and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Prompting is controlling a model's behavior purely through the input text you give it, with no code or weight changes.
examples:
# vague: 'Summarize this article'
# clear: 'Summarize this article in exactly 3 bullet points, each under 15 words, focused on the financial impact only'
commonMistakes: Assuming a model will 'figure out what I meant' the way a human colleague might — being explicit about format, length, and focus consistently produces more reliable, repeatable results than.
lessons.careerRelevance: Instruction clarity is the single highest-leverage prompting skill and the first thing reviewed when debugging an unreliable LLM feature.

lessons.title: Context, constraints & zero/few-shot prompting
objectives: Apply zero-shot and few-shot prompting, and supply the right context/constraints
Explain how zero-shot changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect zero-shot with few-shot prompting and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Zero-shot prompting asks the model to perform a task with no examples, relying purely on instructions. Few-shot prompting includes a small number of example input/output pairs directly in the prompt, which often dramatically improves consistency for tasks with a specific format or style that's hard to describe in words alone.
examples:
# few-shot example pattern:
# 'Classify sentiment.
Text: I love this! -> positive
Text: This is terrible. -> negative
Text: {new_input} -> '
# the two examples teach the FORMAT and STYLE expected, not just the instruction
commonMistakes: Providing few-shot examples that are inconsistent with each other in format or style — the model will often pick up on and reproduce that inconsistency rather than converging on one clean.
lessons.careerRelevance: Few-shot prompting is frequently the single most effective technique for stabilizing an otherwise inconsistent LLM output format.
lessons.explain: Zero-shot prompting asks the model to perform a task with no examples, relying purely on instructions. Few-shot prompting includes a small number of example input/output pairs directly in the prompt, which often dramatically improves consistency for tasks with a specific format or style that's hard to describe in words alone.
lessons.example:
# few-shot example pattern:
# 'Classify sentiment.
Text: I love this! -> positive
Text: This is terrible. -> negative
Text: {new_input} -> '
# the two examples teach the FORMAT and STYLE expected, not just the instruction

lessons.title: Role prompting & structured output
objectives: Use role prompting to set behavior, and request reliably parseable structured output
Explain how role prompting changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect role prompting with structured output and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Role prompting ('You are a senior code reviewer..') sets a frame that shapes tone, vocabulary, and focus without needing to spell out every expectation explicitly.
examples:
# role: 'You are a strict security auditor. Review this code for vulnerabilities only.'
# structured output: 'Respond with ONLY valid JSON: {"vulnerabilities": [...], "severity": "low|medium|high"}'
commonMistakes: Asking for JSON output but not explicitly forbidding extra prose ('Here's your JSON:') around it — this breaks naive parsing; be explicit that the response must be ONLY the JSON, nothing.
lessons.careerRelevance: Structured output is the backbone of virtually every real LLM-powered application feature, not just chat interfaces.
lessons.explain: Role prompting ('You are a senior code reviewer..') sets a frame that shapes tone, vocabulary, and focus without needing to spell out every expectation explicitly.

lessons.title: Prompt decomposition & step-by-step reasoning prompts
objectives: Break a complex task into smaller prompted steps, and use step-by-step reasoning prompts
Explain how prompt decomposition changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect prompt decomposition with step-by-step reasoning prompts and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Complex tasks often work better broken into smaller prompted steps (decomposition) than attempted in one giant prompt — each step is easier to verify and debug independently.
examples:
# decomposition: instead of one prompt doing 'extract data AND validate it AND format a report',
# do 3 separate prompts, each with a narrow, checkable job

# step-by-step reasoning prompt:
# 'Think through this step by step, then give your final answer on the last line.'
commonMistakes: Assuming a single mega-prompt can reliably do everything at once — decomposed steps are each individually easier to test, debug, and improve than one large, hard-to-diagnose prompt.
lessons.careerRelevance: Decomposition is exactly the prompting-level skill that connects directly to the AI Agents track's multi-step workflows.

lessons.title: Prompt templates, testing & versioning
objectives: Build a reusable prompt template and treat prompts as versioned, tested artifacts
Explain how prompt templates changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect prompt templates with prompt testing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A prompt template has fixed instructions with variable slots filled in per request (e.g. `f"Summarize this in {n} sentences: {text}"`), letting you reuse a tested pattern reliably across many inputs.
examples:
PROMPT_TEMPLATE_V3 = "Summarize the following in {n} sentences, focusing on {focus}:\n\n{text}"
# test this template against 10 representative real inputs BEFORE deploying a wording change
# keep V2 available to roll back to if V3 regresses on the test set
commonMistakes: Editing a production prompt directly with no test set to check against — a seemingly small wording tweak can quietly break behavior for edge cases you didn't think to check by hand.
lessons.careerRelevance: Treating prompts as versioned, tested artifacts (not just text you edit ad hoc) is what separates a production LLM feature from a fragile demo.
lessons.explain: A prompt template has fixed instructions with variable slots filled in per request (e.g. `f"Summarize this in {n} sentences: {text}"`), letting you reuse a tested pattern reliably across many inputs.
lessons.example:

# test this template against 10 representative real inputs BEFORE deploying a wording change
# keep V2 available to roll back to if V3 regresses on the test set

lessons.title: Evaluation criteria for prompts
objectives: Define concrete criteria to judge whether a prompt is working well
Explain how prompt evaluation criteria changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect prompt evaluation criteria with test sets and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A prompt is 'good' only relative to explicit criteria: does it reliably produce the right FORMAT (parseable, complete), the right CONTENT (accurate, relevant, appropriately scoped), and consistent behavior across a range of realistic inputs (not just the one example you tried first)?
examples:
# evaluation checklist for a prompt, run against 15-20 representative test inputs:
# - format: valid, parseable, matches schema? (checkable automatically)
# - content: accurate, on-topic, appropriately scoped? (often needs human/LLM-graded review)
# - consistency: does behavior hold across edge cases (empty input, very long input, adversarial input)?
commonMistakes: Judging a prompt as 'working' after trying it on one or two inputs — real prompt evaluation needs a representative test set covering typical AND edge cases before you trust it in production.
lessons.careerRelevance: Building this evaluation discipline is exactly what turns prompt engineering into a real engineering practice rather than trial and error.
lessons.explain: A prompt is 'good' only relative to explicit criteria: does it reliably produce the right FORMAT (parseable, complete), the right CONTENT (accurate, relevant, appropriately scoped), and consistent behavior across a range of realistic inputs (not just the one example you tried first)?

# - content: accurate, on-topic, appropriately scoped? (often needs human/LLM-graded review)
# - consistency: does behavior hold across edge cases (empty input, very long input, adversarial input)?

lessons.title: Guardrails & injection risks
objectives: Identify prompt injection risk and describe basic guardrail strategies
Explain how prompt injection changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect prompt injection with trusted vs untrusted input and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Prompt injection happens when untrusted input (user text, a fetched document) contains text designed to hijack the model's instructions — e.g.
examples:
# vulnerable: directly concatenating a fetched web page into the prompt as if it were trusted
# safer: clearly delimit untrusted content, explicitly instruct the model to treat it as DATA,
# never as new instructions -- and never let it alone trigger a high-privilege action
commonMistakes: Treating any text fed into a prompt (documents, user messages, web content) as automatically safe/trustworthy — anything not directly authored by your own trusted system should be treated as.
lessons.careerRelevance: Prompt injection is now a standard, named security concern in any LLM-application security review, directly relevant to the AI Agents track's security-risk lesson.

lessons.title: Multimodal prompting & when prompting isn't enough
objectives: Prompt models that accept images/audio, and recognize when prompting alone can't solve a problem
Explain how multimodal prompting changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect multimodal prompting with limits of prompting and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Multimodal prompting extends these same principles (clarity, structure, few-shot examples) to inputs that include images or audio alongside text — describing what to look for or listen for just as specifically as you would for text.
examples:
# prompting CAN'T fix: 'the model doesn't know about our internal product launched yesterday' -> needs RAG
# prompting CAN'T fix: 'the model must NEVER output a number over 100' -> needs code-level validation, not just asking nicely
# prompting CAN'T fix: 'send the actual email' -> needs a tool-using agent
commonMistakes: Trying to solve every reliability problem by just rewording the prompt harder — some problems genuinely need a different tool (retrieval, code-level validation, or agentic tool use), not a.
lessons.careerRelevance: Recognizing prompting's limits is exactly what correctly routes you to the RAG and AI Agents tracks that follow.

lessons.title: Iterating on prompts systematically
objectives: Improve a prompt through deliberate, testable iteration
Explain how prompt iteration changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect prompt iteration with systematic testing and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Prompt engineering is rarely right on the first try -- it's an iterative process: write a prompt, test it against real/representative inputs, identify exactly where it fails, adjust one thing, and retest. Treating this like debugging (isolate the failure, change one variable) is far more effective than rewriting the whole prompt randomly hoping it improves.
examples:
# iteration loop:
# 1. write prompt v1, test on 5 real examples
# 2. note exactly which examples failed and how
# 3. change ONE thing (e.g. add a constraint) -> v2
# 4. retest the SAME 5 examples, compare
commonMistakes: Rewriting an entire prompt from scratch after one failure, instead of isolating and changing just the part that's actually causing the problem.
lessons.careerRelevance: Systematic prompt iteration is a real, practical skill distinguishing effective prompt engineers from trial-and-error guessing.

quiz.q: Few-shot prompting primarily helps by:
options: training new model weights
showing example input/output pairs to stabilize format and style
increasing the context window
replacing the need for instructions

quiz.q: Structured output prompting is most important when:
options: a human will read the response directly
your code needs to reliably parse the response
the prompt is very short
using role prompting

quiz.q: Prompt injection risk mainly comes from:
options: the model's training data size
untrusted input containing text designed to hijack instructions
using too few examples
using a small context window

quiz.q: Prompting alone CANNOT reliably:
options: set a tone or role
teach the model new facts it wasn't trained on
request a specific output format
provide examples of desired behavior

quiz.q: A prompt template is best described as:
options: a one-time-use prompt
fixed instructions with variable slots, reused across requests
a type of guardrail only
a model architecture

quiz.q: Why is prompting described as a 'control surface'?
options: prompting has no real effect on model behavior
it's the primary way to steer a model's behavior and output without changing its underlying weights

quiz.q: What does 'ambiguity in = ambiguity out' mean?
options: ambiguous prompts always produce better creative output
a vague or unclear prompt tends to produce a vague or unpredictable response
ambiguity has no effect on output quality
this only applies to few-shot prompting

quiz.q: What is zero-shot prompting?
options: providing many labeled examples before the actual task
asking the model to perform a task with no examples provided, relying on its general capability
training the model from scratch
a synonym for temperature

quiz.q: What is few-shot prompting?
options: providing zero examples
including a small number of examples in the prompt to demonstrate the desired pattern or format
fine-tuning the model's weights
a synonym for zero-shot

quiz.q: Why include constraints in a prompt (e.g. 'answer in under 50 words')?
options: constraints always confuse the model
constraints shape the output format/scope directly, rather than hoping the model infers your implicit expectations
constraints are ignored by all models
constraints only work with few-shot prompting

quiz.q: What is role prompting?
options: asking the model to remember your name
instructing the model to adopt a specific persona or perspective (e.g. 'act as a security reviewer') to shape its response style
a synonym for temperature
only usable with images

quiz.q: What does requesting structured output (like JSON) from a model accomplish?
options: it slows down generation with no benefit
it produces output in a predictable, parseable format that downstream code can reliably process
structured output requests are always ignored
this only works for numeric data

quiz.q: What is schema-constrained generation?
options: generating completely unstructured text
constraining a model's output to conform to a specific structure or schema, improving reliability for downstream parsing
a synonym for zero-shot prompting
only relevant for image generation

quiz.q: What is prompt decomposition?
options: combining multiple tasks into one single instruction
breaking a complex task into smaller, sequential sub-prompts or steps
a synonym for temperature
deleting parts of a prompt randomly

quiz.q: Why do step-by-step reasoning prompts often improve accuracy on complex tasks?
options: they never improve accuracy
encouraging the model to work through intermediate steps explicitly can catch errors that jumping straight to an answer would miss
reasoning prompts only work for math problems
this technique only applies to zero-shot prompting

quiz.q: What does output verifiability mean in the context of reasoning prompts?
options: the output can never be checked
being able to inspect the model's intermediate reasoning steps, not just the final answer, to judge whether the logic holds up
verifiability only applies to structured output
this concept doesn't apply to language models

quiz.q: What is a prompt template?
options: a fixed, unchangeable prompt
a reusable prompt structure with placeholders for variable content, applied consistently across many inputs
a synonym for few-shot examples
only used for image generation prompts

quiz.q: Why version prompts, similar to versioning code?
options: prompt versioning is unnecessary busywork
prompts evolve and changes can affect behavior significantly, so tracking versions helps understand what changed and why
versioning only applies to model weights
prompts never need to change once written

quiz.q: Why maintain a test set for evaluating prompts?
options: test sets are unnecessary for prompts
a consistent set of representative inputs lets you objectively compare whether a prompt change actually improved results
prompts can't be tested systematically
test sets are only relevant for classifiers

quiz.q: What's the difference between format checks and content checks when evaluating prompt output?
options: they're identical checks
format checks verify structural correctness (like valid JSON); content checks verify the actual substance/correctness of the response
format checks are always more important
content checks only apply to few-shot prompts

quiz.q: What is prompt injection?
options: a technique for speeding up inference
malicious or unexpected input designed to override or manipulate a model's intended instructions
a synonym for few-shot prompting
a required part of every prompt

quiz.q: Why distinguish trusted from untrusted input when designing a prompt?
options: there's no meaningful distinction
untrusted input (like user-pasted text) can contain injection attempts, so it needs separate handling from your own trusted instructions
trusted and untrusted input are processed identically by design
this distinction only matters for image prompts

quiz.q: Why validate a model's output before using it downstream?
options: validation is never necessary
models can produce malformed, incomplete, or incorrect output that unvalidated downstream code might mishandle
output is always perfectly formatted
validation only matters for numeric output

quiz.q: What is multimodal prompting?
options: prompting only with text
providing a prompt that combines multiple input types, like text and an image, in a single request
a synonym for zero-shot prompting
only relevant for audio models

quiz.q: What are the limits of prompting alone?
options: prompting can solve any task with the right wording
some tasks need external capabilities prompting alone can't provide, like up-to-date facts (RAG) or multi-step actions (agents)
there are no real limits to prompting

quiz.q: When should you 'reach for RAG' instead of relying purely on prompting?
options: always, for every single task
when the answer depends on specific, current, or proprietary information the model wasn't trained on
RAG should never be used alongside prompting

quiz.q: Why is instruction specificity important in prompt writing?
options: specificity always makes prompts worse

quiz.q: What is the benefit of iterating on a prompt rather than accepting the first version?
options: there's no benefit, first drafts are always sufficient

quiz.q: Why change only one variable at a time when iterating on a prompt?

one-variable-at-a-time is a myth with no practical benefit
